zeroday-ai-autonomous-vulnerability-patc.name: ZeroDay AI
zeroday-ai-autonomous-vulnerability-patc.summary: Autonomous AI agent that detects code vulnerabilities, writes secure patches, and opens GitHub Pull Requests instantly without human intervention.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They assumed the expensive step (generation, review, data entry) should be priced before it runs.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: Autonomous AI agent that detects code vulnerabilities, writes secure patches, and opens GitHub Pull Requests instantly without human intervention.
steal_this: Decide which single action is expensive enough to require a human, and make that gate a schema state transition rather than a prompt request.
Replace chat turns with a scheduled process that wakes on a condition. Patience is a feature nobody else ships.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then ZeroDay AI made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any tool with an expensive generation step

audit.worth_note: The most crowded genre in this corpus — an agent that finds a flaw, writes a patch and opens a pull request — and this entry publishes no repository, no demo and one number with no denominator, so almost none of it can be checked. It earns a row rather than a pile because two decisions on the page are the correct ones for the genre and are named rather than glossed: the pull request is gated on the project's own tests passing inside a sandbox, and the retry loop's real difficulty is stated as *not looping forever*, which is the failure mode that makes an autonomous patcher dangerous. Read it for those two boundaries; do not read the 30 seconds as a result.

assumptions: a container or equivalent isolation to run a target repository's test suite without trusting it — the security-relevant part, and the one the page does not describe
repository write credentials scoped to open PRs but not to merge, which is a policy decision as much as a configuration one
a real scanner or rule set (Semgrep/CodeQL/GoSec class) rather than "ask the model what looks insecure" — otherwise the eval question is unanswerable
a retry budget plus a distinct FAILED/UNVERIFIED outcome, so an exhausted loop is visible rather than absent
clone_cost.why: the demo-able shell (webhook, one model call, one test command, one PR) is a weekend, and that is exactly why the genre is crowded. What is not a weekend: a detector worth trusting for write access, a sandbox that is isolated enough to run untrusted repo tests safely, and a bounded retry policy with a terminal failure state a human can act on.

audit.what_to_steal: Make the verification step able to *refuse*: the agent's output is a pull request only after the target project's unit tests pass in a throwaway container, so "the model wrote something plausible" never becomes a state the system can reach. Then steal the honest framing of the loop around it — the page names the retry bound as the hard part instead of describing the loop as always converging, which is the sentence an autonomous-remediation design usually omits. Third, cheap and specific: a local pre-scan (Gemma, client-side, for syntax errors) before paying for a sandbox run is the same trick as checking a claim against a cache before calling the model — cost the cheap filter first, and only escalate what survives it.
audit.what_breaks_first: The detector, because it is undescribed. Everything downstream is careful — sandbox, tests, PR — but a patcher's ceiling is what it notices, and the page names two finding classes (SQL injection, exposed API keys) with no scanner, no ruleset and no false-negative story, so a miss is invisible by construction: the pipeline reports nothing and looks healthy. Second is the retry budget: "under 30 seconds" and "without causing infinite retry loops" cannot both be true for a hard patch, so on a real failure the run either times out mid-loop or silently gives up, and neither terminal state is published. Third is the trust surface — an agent with write access to repositories and a chat assistant over its own audit log is an approval target, and nothing on the page says who authorises the PR beyond a human clicking.

prior_art.relation: same event, same shape of problem, opposite answer on the trust boundary: Tower checks obligations against live artifacts and keeps UNVERIFIED as a distinct terminal state so it never asserts what it could not see, whereas ZeroDay's agent acts — writes code and opens a PR — with the target project's tests as its only gate. Read together they are the two available designs for "when is an agent allowed to have an opinion".
